concept.name: Market resiliency
concept.definition: The speed at which prices and order-book liquidity return toward equilibrium after a trade or shock displaces them - one of the liquidity dimensions identified by Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002), who describe resiliency as the promptness with which price impacts from transactions are corrected.
concept.intuition: It measures how fast the market heals after being hit by a large order or news.
concept.mechanics: Gauged by the time for spreads and displayed depth to replenish and for transitory price impact to decay after large trades; empirically estimated from quote-replenishment rates and impact-decay dynamics following order-flow shocks.
concept.failure_modes: Resiliency collapses in correlated stress: during the May 2010 Flash Crash liquidity was withdrawn faster than it could be replenished. It is also inherently difficult to measure ex ante rather than after the fact.
concept.misconceptions: A market that has historically bounced back quickly offers no guarantee of doing so in the next stress event; resiliency is regime-dependent, not a fixed property.
concept.example: A block sale knocks a stock down 0.3%; in a resilient market new bids refill the book and the price recovers most of the drop within seconds.

citations.source: Sarr and Lybek, 'Measuring Liquidity in Financial Markets', IMF Working Paper WP/02/232
